“To tell or not to tell”: 55 countries — final report

One model (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct), one story prompt, 55 countries plus a no-country control. Judge: Claude Haiku 5.5 (a pass blind to the country, a pass aware of it, and a second pass that assigns every reason to the approved list of themes).

2. Data quality

Every story is kept in the data and counted. Failures are: language switch (at least one Chinese/Japanese/Korean character in an English story), off-task, refusal or disclaimer, and parse failures of the judge. The main analyses use the valid stories; a robustness check with all stories is reported in section 5.

4. Maps

One variable at a time, for all 55 countries. Value shows the share in each country; Difference from NONE shows the country’s value minus the no-country control (red: higher than NONE, blue: lower). Next to each map the same data are shown with 95% Wilson intervals and the NONE value as a dashed line. With 55 countries and about 80 stories each, most differences between neighbouring shades are within noise: read the intervals, not the colours. Hover for the exact values.

5. Does the country matter?

Three comparisons, all with the Jensen–Shannon distance (in bits) between distributions of decision, scene resolution and main-reason theme (approved list), and each compared with the distance that sampling noise alone produces (country labels, or the named/not-named label, shuffled across stories 1000 times). (a) Do the stories with a country, pooled, differ from NONE? (b) Do countries differ from one another? (c) Which countries stand out from the other countries? A further view, (d), compares each country with NONE after giving NONE the country’s size. P-values are empirical, descriptive and never confirmatory; those per country are corrected for 55 comparisons (Benjamini–Hochberg).

(a) and (b): named vs not named, and heterogeneity among countries

6. Country × reason, and how country-specific each reason is

Each reason in a story is assigned to a theme (the approved list, assigned by a second Haiku pass), to one of the 24 bottom-up clusters of section 9 (an exploratory reading aid), or to the provisional sphere given in the first pass; all three labelings are kept in the data. The unit is either the main reason only (first in the judge’s list, as agreed) or all reasons (about 3 per story, more counts but the reasons of one story are not independent).

7. Inventory of cultural markers

Everything the model put in a story that the judge (pass B, aware of the requested country) listed as a cultural element, plus the protagonist, friend and partner names and the main place. Counts are stories (an element is counted once per story), valid stories only. “Postcard” markers are those that recur often and concentrate in one country; generic elements (common first names, tea, café) are spread across many countries and also appear in NONE.

What kinds of marker each country’s stories contain

Share of a country’s valid stories with at least one element of each type, and the number of distinct elements. Row order as in the country list.

8. Stories by pattern

Stories are shown exactly as generated. Selection rule: 3 stories drawn at random with a fixed seed from the valid stories with a country, from different countries. Each shows the judge’s quote for the decision and the reasons.

9. Reasons: provisional spheres, approved themes and bottom-up clusters

Pass A collected each reason as free text with a provisional sphere. After wave 1 the free texts were grouped bottom-up (embeddings with BAAI/bge-m3, k-means with k = 24 fitted on wave 1; the wave 2 reasons are assigned to the nearest wave-1 centre, so the clusters did not change) and, from the clusters, a list of themes was proposed and approved. A second Haiku pass then assigned every reason to the approved list: 9 bottom-up themes plus 7 culture-related categories kept as theory-driven (religion, honour, family/community, law/institutions, privacy, fidelity, practical self-interest) plus “other”. The provisional sphere and the approved theme are both kept in the data.
